claims.text: ``harness._recall`` measures substring containment in a context slice. It is honest about that and useful for it: it grades the SLICER. It never looks at a patch, so it cannot say whether a change is CORRECT -- and with an empty ``must_include`` it returns 1.0 vacuously.
claims.why: Claims about harness._recall are in another module; this chunk contains no such code.

claims.text: Before this module there was no correctness evaluator in this repo at all, and the consequence was measured, not feared: the gate's rejection rate against the three known-bad changes of a single day was 0/3, three green suites sat over three live escapes, and an A/B experiment shipped with both arms passing a gate that ran no tests.
claims.why: Historical claims about prior gate behavior cannot be verified from this chunk.

claims.text: Every outcome this evaluator can report. Five facts, deliberately not one boolean -- "the patch did not fix it" and "the patch broke a regression test" are different engineering problems and must not collapse.
claims.why: OUTCOMES is a tuple of five distinct strings.

claims.text: Statuses that PROVE a node did not pass. ``skipped`` is deliberately NOT here: a skip is not evidence of failure any more than it is evidence of success, and treating it as either is how a vacuous green gets minted. ``missing`` is not here either -- a node id that does not exist refutes the TASK, it does not demonstrate a bug.
claims.why: PROVEN_NOT_PASSING is a frozenset containing only failed, error, and collect_error; skipped and missing are absent.

claims.text: Statuses carrying no verdict at all -> ``could_not_run``.
claims.why: NO_VERDICT is a frozenset containing only not_run.

claims.text: NOW A THIN SHELL OVER ``daedalus.primary_tree``. It used to be a second implementation, and its own docstring claimed it "reuses rather than re-discovers" the finding in ``spine/attempt.py::_identity``. It reused the FINDING and not the CODE, and the two copies had already diverged on the case that matters most: this one returned the path on ``OSError`` ("cannot compare identities; the lexical test stands") while attempt.py refused it. A guard that fails OPEN where its twin fails CLOSED is the ``lane_for_host`` disease -- one question, two predicates, agreeing until the day they do not. Measured 2026-07-29: a non-existent target under a DOS device or UNC-admin-share spelling passed here and was refused there.
claims.why: The historical behavior of the old implementation and the exact behavior of assert_write_allowed are not in this chunk; only the delegation is visible.

claims.text: ``assert_write_allowed`` also resolves symlinks and ``..``, which the lexical ``abspath``/``normpath`` pair above never did.

claims.text: A task's ``test_overlay`` is data. ``../../daedalus/spine/attempt.py`` is a perfectly ordinary-looking string, and writing it would put task-chosen bytes into the developer's checkout.
claims.why: The claim about what would happen if the guard were absent is not testable in this chunk.

claims.text: THE ABSOLUTE-PATH BRANCH BELOW IS A FAST PATH, NOT A GUARD, and it is labelled that way because a comment that reads like a guard gets trusted like one. Measured by disabling it: the containment comparison underneath catches every case it catches, so no test changed verdict -- ``os.path.join`` lets an absolute right-hand side win, and the result then fails the "is it under the worktree" test anyway (``C:/x/y`` -> outside; ``/etc/passwd`` -> ``C:\\etc\\passwd``, outside; ``C:relative.py``, which is drive-RELATIVE, joins to a path INSIDE the worktree and is harmless). It is kept only because it answers the common case with a more specific message. The containment comparison is the thing actually holding the line.
claims.why: The claim that disabling the absolute-path branch does not change verdicts is a measurement claim not reproducible from this chunk; the containment comparison is present and appears to enforce the boundary.

observations.what: The module docstring makes many claims about evaluation flow, but this chunk only contains guards and constants; the flow is in later chunks.
_git_read uses subprocess.run with capture_output=True but does not set text=True, so output is raw bytes as claimed.

_safe_join normalizes the worktree with os.path.abspath and os.path.normpath, and the containment check uses _key with os.sep; the absolute-path fast path raises OverlayEscape before the containment check.
_git_in_worktree's body is not present in this chunk; the docstring claim about _refuse_primary_checkout being used cannot be verified here.
